entries.title: Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
entries.summary: False and misleading claims are raising questions about the integrity of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. DW Fact Check takes a closer look.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt

September 6, 2026

False and misleading claims are raising questions about the integrity of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. DW Fact Check takes a closer look.

On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II. 

In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.

DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.  

Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.

Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots

Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.  

A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."

The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube. 

Verdict: False

There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.

They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.  

The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign. 

Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election. 

Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system

Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud

Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.  

"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another. 

Verdict: False

DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud. 

The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.

Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".

One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."

Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.

"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.

DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.

Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections

Did Halle start counting ballots too early?

Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist. 

Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".

Verdict: Misleading

The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.  

Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.

The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."

The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting. 

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD secures huge lead in key vote
entries.summary: The far-right AfD has taken a massive lead at the Saxony-Anhalt election, although it was not clear if it will be able to form government. The party's state leader said the result sends "a signal to Berlin." Follow DW.
entries.content:
Louis Oelofse|

Richard Connorwith dpa, AFP, AP, KNA, Reuters |

Zac Crellin|

Felix Tamsut|

Darko Janjevic

The far-right AfD has taken a massive lead at the Saxony-Anhalt election, although it was not clear if it will be able to form government. The party's state leader said the result sends "a signal to Berlin." Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
  • AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
  • Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
  • Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification

It is election day in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state. Follow all the developments here.

Skip next section WATCH: AfD celebrates, CDU reels from election setback

WATCH: AfD celebrates, CDU reels from election setback

The far-right AfD party has achieved a huge victory in the election in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. But it appears it has not got enough votes to take control of the government there.

Skip next section AfD's Siegmund says victory in Saxony-Anhalt will 'shake all of Germany'

AfD's Siegmund says victory in Saxony-Anhalt will 'shake all of Germany'

The AfD has "written history" with the Saxony-Anhalt result, the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund told supporters on Sunday evening.

"Our vision for 2026 has come true," Siegmund said in his victory speech in Magdeburg. "We are going to get our country back, and we are starting with Saxony-Anhalt."

He said the result would "shake all of Germany" and send a "self-confident signal" across the country.

"The people in this country are giving us their trust. We will not disappoint them," Siegmund said. "We will not become like these other parties. We are the Alternative for Germany."

Siegmund also attacked media coverage of his party, saying the AfD had shown that "no matter how much fake news there was about us, we cannot be divided."

"In other parties you hide the chancellor. In the AfD, we stand together," he added,

The remark appeared to target the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which kept Chancellor Friedrich Merz largely out of its campaign in Saxony-Anhalt.

Skip next section FACT CHECK: Russian disinformation campaign fabricates election fraud media reports

FACT CHECK: Russian disinformation campaign fabricates election fraud media reports

Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the "CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.

"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.

Verdict: False

DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. Each of the videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, German public broadcaster ARD, Wired magazine, and the BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.

The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.

Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit."

Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.

"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.

One of the videos claims T-Online reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."

DW Fact Check has debunked other Russian disinformation targeting German elections: Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections

Skip next section Saxony Anhalt result 'inspiring,' AfD Bundestag member tells DW

Saxony Anhalt result 'inspiring,' AfD Bundestag member tells DW

AfD Bundestag member Markus Frohmaier called the far-right party's results in the Saxony Anhalt election "inspiring" and praised Ulrich Sigmund's campaign performance as "amazing."

When asked by DW about the party's priorities going ahead, Frohmaier mentioned "illegal mass migration" and internal security.

"I think the AfD is the only party that's able to solve these issues," he said, adding that he believes the result sends out a message to the world that "Germany is back."

"Germany is able to protect national interests," Frohmaier said, adding that this has not been the case for "many decades."

Frohmaier said he still hopes the party will manage to secure a majority of seats without having to join a coalition with other parties.

Skip next section AfD's lead candidate Siegmund rejects leftist BSW as coalition partner

AfD's lead candidate Siegmund rejects leftist BSW as coalition partner

The lead AfDcandidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, Ulrich Siegmund, has poured cold water on the prospect of cooperation with the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Siegmund said the BSW was "not part of the solution but part of the problem."

The remark comes after BSW's Claudia Wittig signaled openness to working with the AfD on individual policy issues.

Wittig argued that excluding the AfD entirely from government would be "completely undemocratic" given its strong election result. At the same time, she rejected both Siegmund and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) candidate Sven Schulze as premier, instead calling for a nonpartisan head of government.

Most of the other parties have rejected the possibility of working with the AfD.

Skip next section Preliminary results confirm AfD far ahead of rivals

Preliminary results confirm AfD far ahead of rivals

The latest preliminary results, published on Sunday evening, put the AfD at 44.2%, slightly less than the 44.5% projected by the exit polls.

At the same time, the AfD's closest rival, the CDU, seems set to win 18% — half a percentage point less than predicted earlier.

Skip next section FACT CHECK: Fake video claims to show AfD ballots crossed out

FACT CHECK: Fake video claims to show AfD ballots crossed out

Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.

A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."

The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across X as well as on YouTube.

Verdict: False

There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.

The ballots are also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures they can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.

The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.

DW Fact Check has also debunked other false claims around Germany's postal voting system: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged

Skip next section Jewish council leader 'personally appalled' by AfD result

Jewish council leader 'personally appalled' by AfD result

Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, reacted with alarm to the Alternative for Germany’s strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt.

"The outcome of the election is still open, but one thing is already clear: A party officially classified as confirmed far-right extremist is only just short of governing a German state on its own," Schuster told the Welt newspaper.

Schuster's comments were in reference to the 2023 decision made by Germany's domestic intelligence agency BfV, which declared the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch a confirmed far-right and extremist  over antisemitic, anti-Muslim and racist statements made by its functionaries.

"I am personally appalled by this election result," Schuster said, adding that the AfD’s goals had been clear for months.

The AfD’s program in Saxony-Anhalt includes a tougher deportation policy, major changes to school curricula and integration policies, a stronger emphasis on nationalism and traditional German identity, and restrictions on some cultural and public institutions.

"Those who voted for it today — despite or because of these goals — bear responsibility for this result," Schuster said.

"The damage that the so-called Alternative for Germany could now cause if it assumes responsibility is immense," he said, arguing that education is crucial to preserving an open society and fighting antisemitism.

Skip next section AfD's Chrupalla claims mandate to govern after Saxony-Anhalt victory

AfD's Chrupalla claims mandate to govern after Saxony-Anhalt victory

Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Tino Chrupalla  says his party secured a mandate to govern with its strong election result in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We have halved the CDU, so from that point of view it’s a great evening," Chrupalla told journalists in Magdeburg, referring to an earlier remark by Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leader and chancellor Friedrich Merz that AfD's result could be cut in half.

Chrupalla called the outcome "sensational."

"Ulrich Siegmund will be the new premier of Saxony-Anhalt," he said. "From here, we will change Germany."

If the party falls short of an absolute majority, Chrupalla said it would be open to talks and even suggested an AfD minority government could be tolerated by other parties.

Lead candidate Siegmund, however, later rejected that option, saying there would be "no arrangements involving a minority government or anything like that." He said the AfD would, in principle. be open to a coalition partner willing to change migration and energy policy, but that he currently saw no such party.

Skip next section No left-wing cooperation with the AfD, Left co-chair says

No left-wing cooperation with the AfD, Left co-chair says

Co-leader of Germany's Left Party Heidi Reichinnek said her party will not cooperate with the AfD in the wake of the Saxony-Anhalt elections under any circumstances.

She called the AfD a "right-wing extremist" party.

"We will do our best to prevent the AfD from reaching a position of power, but we cannot do this on our own," Reichinnek told German public broadcaster ARD, while also calling all other parties to keep up the so-called "firewall," the policy of excluding any political cooperation with the AfD.

"Many people here are scared, people with migrant backgrounds, queer people. I'd like to tell them: You are not alone," Reichinnek said.

Skip next section BSW open to working with AfD on policy issues

BSW open to working with AfD on policy issues

The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has signaled that it could cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on individual policy issues in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We will always decide on the substance," BSW lead candidate Claudia Wittig told Germany's public broadcaster ARD.

She used the example of energy prices, saying that such issues "can be done together with the AfD," while there may be less common ground in other areas.

Wittig also argued that, given the AfD’s strong result, it would be "completely undemocratic not to involve them in government in some way."

At the same time, she rejected both AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund and incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU) Premier Sven Schulze as potential heads of the next state government.

"We want a nonpartisan premier," Wittig said.

She also argued that her leftist populist party could help bridge an increasingly polarized political landscape.

The BSW, founded in 2024 around former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht, advocates for greater social and economic equality but also calls for more restrictive positions on migration and criticizes  Germany’s foreign policy.

Current projections put the party at exactly 5.0%, right on the threshold needed to win seats, but a minor shift in numbers could see it miss out on the state parliament.

Skip next section Greens hail gains, warn of AfD surge in Saxony-Anhalt

Greens hail gains, warn of AfD surge in Saxony-Anhalt

There was massive jubilation at the Greens' election event in Magdeburg when the party's own result appeared on screen, DW correspondent Giulia Saudelli reported. Some staff members were in tears of joy and relief.

The Greens reached 8.9% in the first projection, significantly outperforming pre-election surveys that had generally put them at around 5%. If the result holds, it would be a historic result for the party in Saxony-Anhalt.

Lead candidate Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said civil society had placed its hopes in the Greens.

"We will not disappoint that hope," she said, adding that the party would "always be the antagonist of the right" in the state parliament.

Greens co-leader Felix Banaszak also welcomed his own party's result.

"Many had already written off the Greens," Banaszak said, adding that the party was now on course for its best-ever state election result in Saxony-Anhalt. "That fills me with joy and pride."

At the same time, he said he was deeply concerned by the AfD’s strong gains.

"These are dramatic conditions that are emerging here," Banaszak said.

DW reporter Saudelli also reported shocked faces as party members saw the AfD and CDU results and considered the difficult task of forming a government without the far-right Alternative for Germany.

Skip next section CDU campaigners watch painful results roll in

CDU campaigners watch painful results roll in

In the ballroom of the hotel in Magdeburg serving as the CDU's headquarters, "there are almost as many journalists as party officials," says DW correspondent Bernd Riegert.

Only die-hard supporters came out to witness the predictable debacle of Germany's center-right conservatives.

"It's a bit like being in the waiting room at the dentist," a CDU supporter said with a bitter smile. "You know it's going to hurt, but you can't run away."

It's not yet clear who will form the next state government. What is certain for now is that CDU, with its share of the vote halved, is no longer the dominant political force in Saxony-Anhalt.

"A disaster, a disaster," murmured a young CDU supporter who put up posters during the campaign.

Skip next section The Saxony-Anhalt projected seats: What do they mean?

The Saxony-Anhalt projected seats: What do they mean?

The projected seat results suggest the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is set to win 39 seats in the new Saxony-Anhalt parliament, three short of an absolute majority and the ability to govern on its own.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's ruling CDU is projected to win 16 seats, its worst result in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification. The Greens and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) are expected to receive eight and seven seats, respectively.

While the results are subject to change, it currently appears difficult for either the AfD or the other parties to form a coalition.

According to a poll by German public broadcaster ARD, the only party where the majority of voters believe the AfD should be in government is the left-wing populist BSW, which is projected to win five seats in parliament. However, only 57% of BSW supporters hold that view.

Skip next section Schulze admits major CDU defeat in Saxony-Anhalt

Schulze admits major CDU defeat in Saxony-Anhalt

Saxony-Anhalt premier and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) lead candidate Sven Schulze said exit polls showed the scale of the setback for his party, putting the conservatives at 18.5%.

"That is democracy, people have sent a signal," he said.

He congratulated the Alternative for Germany (AfD) on winning the election and said it was now on the CDU to find a way to deal with the outcome.

Schulze described the campaign as exceptionally tough.

"I have never experienced such an election campaign in my 25 years in politics," he said.

Meanwhile, CDU Secretary-General Franziska Hoppermann ruled out any cooperation with the AfD.

"We will not work with radicals, especially not with right-wing radicals," she told the German state broadcaster.

She also dismissed speculation about this result affecting the future of Germany's chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz.

"No, there will be no discussion," she said.

Meanwhile, Chancellery Minister Nina Warken, a close ally of Merz, described the result as a "turning point" for the CDU and a "very, very difficult result." She said reforms launched by the ruling coalition on the federal level had yet to take full effect.

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact
entries.summary: The election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government. Pollsters point to dissatisfaction with Chancellor Merz as one reason for his party's poor showing.
entries.content:
Germany

Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact

September 6, 2026

The election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government. Pollsters point to dissatisfaction with Chancellor Merz as one reason for his party's poor showing.

Only 1.6 million eligible voters were called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, September 6. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

For weeks it was clear that the vote had become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

The in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party  won the election, doubling its percentage compared to the last election five years ago, while the ruling CDU lost half of its support. If the AfD now manages to form a government, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.

A threat to Chancellor Friedrich Merz?

Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW before the election. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

Koschmieder also predicted that a strong showing by the AfD would intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist. The CDU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.

Most analysts believe that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party.

Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

Merz: Government stability not at risk



The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.

But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.

SPD hopes for success in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

What about the Social Democrats? They have remained at around 8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt. This is a great improvement on what was being predicted six months ago.

In addition, the Social Democrat premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, has good odds of a renewed mandate in state parliament elections there on September 20. The SPD has made a strong comeback in the polls in the coastal state since last year; with around 30% of the vote, they could form a government with the Left Party, the CDU or potentially both.

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on September 3, and updated and republished to include the Saxony-Anhalt election results on September 6.

entries.title: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
entries.summary: Ahead of Germany's state elections in September, rumors began circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's why they're wrong.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged

September 6, 2026

Ahead of Germany's state elections in September, rumors began circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's why they're wrong.

Stakes are high in Germany's three September state elections. Saxony-Anhalt was first and voters handed a strong result to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a "confirmed right-wing extremist organization", could become Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

Mail-in voting, or "Briefwahl," has become an increasingly common feature of German elections. But the rise in mail-in ballots has been followed by a renewed wave of speculation and claims questioning the security and integrity of postal vote.

DW Fact check examined a sample of claims circulating online and assessed what the available evidence shows.

Does postal voting manipulate election results?

Claim: Cases of fraud involving postal ballots prove that postal voting is unreliable.

This claim recurrently appeared in posts about postal voting that DW Fact check reviewed on social media platforms including TikTok, X and Facebook.

Some posts point to individual cases of electoral fraud involving postal ballots and present them as evidence that the system as a whole is flawed. One verified account on X using the AfD logo, for example, cited two cases — a mail-in vote being cast on behalf of an elderly woman with dementia, and hundreds of voters in Magdeburg receiving multiple ballots — before calling postal voting defective and demanding immediate reforms.

DW Fact check: Misleading. Individual cases of fraud, errors or violations do not demonstrate that the entire postal voting system is unreliable or that it has affected the outcome of an election.

The post by the X account with the AfD logo refers to two real incidents, but does so in a misleading way. The claim about an elderly woman may refer to a case in Dessau, where police recently investigated an alleged vote cast on behalf of a 95-year-old woman with "severe dementia" but found no evidence of manipulation. The other incident occurred in Magdeburg, where 440 voters did receive duplicate ballots for the September 6 election ; however, the duplicates were invalidated and could not be used to cast additional valid votes.

Cases of electoral misconduct involving postal ballots have occurred in postal voting, as they have with voting at polling stations. In one case in Dresden, a man manipulated absentee ballots during the 2024 local and state elections, primarily in favor of the far-right Free Saxons party as well as the AfD. And in Bavaria, a former mayor was accused of manipulating postal voting documents in a March 2026 local election.

There have also been documented mistakes, administrative problems and delays in the handling of postal ballots in previous German elections. A 2021 study examining postal voting in German federal elections between 1998 and 2017 found that these weaknesses were primarily related to organization and logistics. Researcher Daniel Hellmann of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg said, however, that the research was still ongoing.

But such problems are not evidence of widespread fraud or of postal ballots being manipulated on a scale capable of changing an election result.

The 2021 study concluded that postal voting in Germany was secure overall. It found that none of the incidents examined could have changed an election result by even a single seat.

"If problems have occurred, they have generally been reviewed through legal channels and proportionate consequences have been imposed," Lukas Stötzer, an election researcher at the University of Witten/Herdecke in western Germany, told DW. "The postal voting system works and is secure, and that's why it is becoming more popular."

Postal voting easy to manipulate?

Claim: Postal votes are easily manipulated during counting.

"It can be assumed that postal voting in Saxony-Anhalt will massively distort the election result, This is also relatively easy to do, and the checks on postal voting are laughable," wrote one user on X with about 130,000 followers on August 14. 

This claim was also a recurring theme among the posts reviewed by DW Fact check, with some of the content presented in satirical, AI-generated cartoons. The AI-generated video depicted here on TikTok and labelled satire, for example, shows a man involved in counting ballots simply altering the votes from AfD to the center-right CDU party, and then calling a man named "Friedrich" — presumably Chancellor Friedrich Merz — to say that he had "everything under control." 

DW Fact check: False. Germany has detailed procedures governing the handling and counting of postal ballots. Postal votes are transported, stored and opened according to established rules, and their counting takes place publicly.

Members of the public are generally allowed to observe the election process, including the counting of votes, without having to demonstrate a particular interest or affiliation. This applies to postal ballot counting as well.

That means election officials do not simply open postal ballots and count them behind closed doors. The process is conducted by election boards, whose work can be observed by members of the public and each parties' representatives.

In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD Christa Dieckmann, Saxony-Anhalt's state election commissioner, pointed to public observation as an important safeguard. "The best way to ensure the fairness of the election is to come to the polling station as an observer for elections as the basis for choosing a legitimate government," she said.

DW Fact check also encountered numerous claims promoting what has been dubbed the "nursing home theory," which alleges that elderly people who are unable to vote in person may not be casting their ballots freely, but could instead be pressured or influenced by certain political parties or caregivers.

DW Fact check has investigated similar claims in the past, many of which have been promoted by AfD politicians. It has found no substantial evidence to support the broader allegation that postal voting in nursing homes is systematically manipulated or that elderly voters are routinely pressured into voting for particular parties.

A familiar claim beyond Germany

The doubts surrounding postal voting are not unique to Germany. Similar claims have surfaced during elections in other democracies, often becoming entangled with broader political battles over the legitimacy of elections.

During the 2020 US presidential election, President Donald Trump repeatedly claimed that expanded mail-in voting would lead to widespread fraud. Fact-checkers documented and debunked repeated false and exaggerated claims about the security of mail ballots. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is again seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots, measures that have faced repeated legal challenges.

Election researcher Stötzer said such claims can become part of a broader political strategy to undermine trust in democratic institutions.

"Right-wing populist parties strategically fuel these doubts," Stötzer said, adding that such claims can later be used to justify electoral law changes that benefit those parties.

He said the immediate impact of such allegations may be limited. But if they are repeated election after election, the longer-term consequences could be more serious.

"Public trust in electoral institutions could suffer," Stötzer said. Election results that are considered undesirable could then routinely be attributed to alleged irregularities in postal voting.

This is a collaborative project between ARD-faktenfinder, and DW Fact check. It was first published on September 4, and updated and republished on September 6.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler and Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong
entries.summary: The AfD has emerged as the strongest party in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt by a wide margin. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?
entries.content:
Germany

Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong

September 6, 2026

The AfD has emerged as the strongest party in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt by a wide margin. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?

Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage. 

Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is also home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still accounts for around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the Elbe River, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.

Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, international attention is now turning to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government after the Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, won in a landslide on September 6.

Can the AfD rule the state?

The far-right AfD has taken a massive lead at the Saxony-Anhalt election, but it was not immediately clear if it will be able to form government. The party's state leader said the result sends "a signal to Berlin." The ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since German reunification in 1990, has lost half of its support. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) which has failed to secure representation by falling underneath the threshhold of 5%.

The state office for the protection of the constitution has classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters. 

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as state premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.

Saxony-Anhalt's unusual political history

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt was also at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party.

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.

What's driving AfD support in Saxony-Anhalt?

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in the state feel with developments in Germany. Many jobs disappeared in the years following reunification, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt also faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the state's Statistical Office, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.

What would AfD rule mean for Saxony-Anhalt?

According to many observers, the success of the far-right DVU some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy program.

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of the Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded.

"I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely," he said. In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script," he said.

The new parliament will convene on October 6, the weeks leading up to this date will see difficult negotiations to form a majority for a new government.

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 24, and updated following the election on September 6.

entries.title: Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill several despite truce
entries.summary: Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun has appealed to the international community to "take immediate action to stop these violations" of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon.
entries.content:
Lebanon

Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill several despite truce

September 6, 2026

Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun has appealed to the international community to "take immediate action to stop these violations" of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon.

At least four people were killed in Israeli strikes on Lebanon on Sunday, which comes despite a ceasefire between the two countries, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.

The Lebanese officials also said around 20 other people, including children, were wounded in the strikes.

The office of Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun called the strikes a "dangerous escalation" that targeted "purely civilian administrations and health centers."

"President Aoun held the Israeli side fully responsible for this ongoing escalation, calling on the United States and the international community to take immediate action to stop ​these violations and hold the perpetrators accountable," his aides said in a statement.

In turn, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the strikes were a response to "a blatant violation" by Hezbollah militants.

"Terrorists from the Hezbollah terrorist organization launched two drones towards IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone in southern Lebanon," the military said in a statement, adding that there were no reports of Israeli soldiers wounded.

What do we know about the strikes?

Early on Sunday morning, the Israeli military issued an online evacuation alert for Arab Salim, saying it identified a "Hezbollah facility" there.

Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said the Israeli military subsequently carried out a strike on the building mentioned in the original evacuation warning.

NNA also reported that "enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it." Two women were killed in the strike.

Another two people were killed in Israeli strikes near the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which lies on the edge of Israel's "security zone" that it occupies in southern Lebanon.

Lebanon's Health Ministry said an Israeli strike "totally destroyed" a disused hospital. The Health Ministry called the incident "another grave violation of international humanitarian law."

The Israeli military said its targets included what it described as a Hezbollah command center inside a building that was previously used as a hospital, as well as a weapons depot.

"The strikes were carried out in response to Hezbollah’s attempted attack yesterday in the Ali Taher Ridge area and to remove threats posed by Hezbollah," it said.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Kiyv after Putin talks
entries.summary: The two US offcials are meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, with national security advisors the UK, France, and Germany reportedly also in Ukraine for talks.
entries.content:
Ukraine

US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Kiyv after Putin talks

September 6, 2026

The two US offcials are meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, with national security advisors the UK, France, and Germany reportedly also in Ukraine for talks.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made their first official visit to Ukraine on Sunday as part of fresh efforts toward peace with Russia.

As Ukraine's airspace remains closed due to the conflict, the pair arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland, having spent more than three hours in talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier.

Putin had declared a three-day ceasefire to ensure the envoys' safety.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine's peace proposals are ready

Ahead of the visit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media that Kyiv is ready for a “constructive” discussion with its US counterparts.

“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer," he wrote. "Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared.”

Reuters news agency reported that national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France and Germany were also in Kyiv for talks with the US envoys, citing a source familiar with the matter.

After meeting Witkoff and Kushner, Zelenskyy said talks were focusing on military aid, including Patriot missiles and other armaments Ukraine would need in the following months.

"If the war drags on until winter — and that is how things currently look — we will need a 'winter package'," he said.

The Ukrainian president also expressed gratitude that representatives of European nations were in Kyiv.

"Here we are all on the same side," he said.

What did Russia say about Moscow talks?

Momentum by US President Donald Trump to end the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict has stalled in recent months after talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January failed to produce a result.

Despite hopes of a breakthrough with the Russian leader on Saturday, there were no announcements after the meeting.

Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow talks as constructive, frank, and useful but didn't discuss specific outcomes.

Ushakov said the talks also focused on economic issues and potentially large Russia-US projects.

During previous talks, negotiators have struggled to bring both sides together on a range of key issues, including the future of the industrial Donbas region of eastern Ukraine.

Ukraine war escalating in recent months

For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and Washington are crucial to deterring Russia ​from further aggression.

Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, told the New York Times last weekend that he did not expect the fighting to end before spring 2027.

He also predicted further Russian strategic air strikes on Ukraine this winter.

The war has escalated in recent months, with Putin seeking the complete conquest of Donbas and Russian drones targeting the Ukrainian capital.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russia's energy sector. It has also targeted online retailers deep inside Russia to try and bring the war home to the public.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: India news: Rahul Gandhi backs student protests in Maharashtra
entries.summary: Opposition Rahul Gandhi has said that students are "tormented" by the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. The Congress politician has demanded immediate action into the demands of Maharashtra student protesters. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: Rahul Gandhi backs student protests in Maharashtra

Published September 5, 2026last updated September 6, 2026

Opposition Rahul Gandhi has said that students are "tormented" by the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. The Congress politician has demanded immediate action into the demands of Maharashtra student protesters. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Rahul Gandhi has said that every demand from students for their successful future 'is justified' amid Maharashtra student demonstrations
  • Flood threat looms in Bihar
  • Preparations for the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi are entering the final phase, with a week left to go

Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India on Saturday, September 5 and Sunday September 6.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Building collapses near Delhi student hub, rescue operation underway

Building collapses near Delhi student hub, rescue operation underway

A rescue effort was ongoing in New Delhi on Sunday afternoon after a multistory building collapsed, killing at least 1 person.

The Delhi fire department said that it received a call around 1:30 pm local time (8:00 UTC) that a building had come down in Satya Niketan, following which rescue teams were mobilized.

The densely populated area is situated near the southern campus of Delhi University and is popular among students for accommodation.

A total of six people have been rescued so far and shifted to hospitals, police said. Local media reports said that several people are feared to be trapped.

Police said the five-story building was 40 to 50 years was being used as accommodation. Repair work was going on in the basement at the time of the collapse.

The cause of the collapse was not immediately known.

Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said she was "deeply concerned" by the incident, adding that a multi-agency rescue operation was being carried out "on a war footing."

"Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped and provide immediate assistance to the affected families," Gupta said, informing that the building adjacent to the collapsed structure had been vacated as a precautionary measure.

Skip next section Flood threat looms in Bihar

Flood threat looms in Bihar

The water level of the Ganges river in the eastern state of Bihar's Patna continues to rise, leading to flood-like situations in low-lying areas around the riverbanks.

Officials said on Sunday that the water level of the river breached a crucial flood mark at Gandhi Ghat in Patna, triggering an alert from the authorities for downstream areas.

Authorities have advised people residing in the risk-prone regions to move to higher ground and the situation is being continuously monitored, news agency ANI reported.

Meanwhile, India's weather agency has forecasted more rainfall for Bihar.

The swelling waters of various rivers in Bihar have affected over 1.9 million people in 11 of the state's districts, news agency PTI reported, citing officials.

On Saturday, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Chaudhary conducted an aerial survey of some of the vulnerable areas to assess the flood situation.

He said in a statement that flood prevention and safety of the people was the "topmost priority," adding that necessary instructions had been issued to officials on relief and rescue operations.

The leader of opposition in the state legislature, Rashtriya Janata Dal's (RJD) Tejashwi Yadav, on Sunday called for aid from the central government, along with assistance from the country's Air Force in distributing relief materials to the affected areas.

Skip next section Congress' Rahul Gandhi says Maharashtra student protest reflects 'shattered' trust in system

Congress' Rahul Gandhi says Maharashtra student protest reflects 'shattered' trust in system

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has voiced support for students protesting in Maharashtra against alleged irregularities in a state-level recruitment examination.

"Thousands of students are on the streets, protesting peacefully — the reason isn't just one exam or recruitment, but a trust that's been shattered by the entire system," Gandhi said in a statement on X as he called on the government to listen to the protesters' demands and act.

"Otherwise, this echo of the students will only grow louder until justice is served," the senior Congress party leader said.

Why are the Maharashtra student demonstrations about?

Gandhi's remarks come as the Maharashtra government initiated a probe into an alleged paper leak of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission's (MPSC) Food and Drug Administration examination for Drug Inspector posts.

The offline exam was held on March 22, following which there were complaints that some candidates had allegedly received the question paper or questions beforehand.

Aspirants said that their complaints were not looked into. The recruitment process was completed and the MPSC published a merit list of 488 candidates.

However, the commission later canceled the recruitment process and in a statement cited a police inquiry which prima facie indicated that a candidate had got hold of the question paper before the exam and benefited from it.

On Saturday, the Maharashtra government also constituted a high-level committee to take full stock of the existing recruitment exam system in the country's second-most populous state.

The committee is tasked with suggesting measures to make the screening process more transparent, secure, reliable and candidate-friendly.

Tribal students' protest

In recent days, several parts of Maharashtra also witnessed a protest by tribal students — including a hunger strike — over poor conditions in student hostels, student safety and recruitment to some 12,500 vacant posts reserved for tribal communities.

The protesters' demands were accepted by the Maharashtra government, leading to the hunger strike being withdrawn.

On Sunday, Rahul Gandhi railed against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads the government in Maharashtra.

"Whether it's the central or state government, every student is tormented by the BJP regime," he alleged.

"Paper leaks, stalled recruitments, the unbearable cost of education, inhumane conditions in hostels, food like poison ...and now, they've seized control of a constitutional body like MPSC and destroyed its credibility," Gandhi, who is the leader of opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, said.

The protests in Maharashtra come after a massive Gen Z-led protest demanding an overhaul of India's examination system, rocked the country in July. The demonstrations marked one of the biggest public challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's three-term rule and culminated with the resignation of the then education minister.

Skip next section Welcome back

Welcome back

It's a rainy Sunday morning in New Delhi and we are back with our weekend coverage of all the developments creating a buzz in India.

Follow along as we bring you more.

Skip next section WATCH — Can India revive its repair culture and curb e-waste?

WATCH — Can India revive its repair culture and curb e-waste?

Many Indians used to get electronic goods fixed, but now many products cannot be mended. A built-in obsolescence has broken the country's electronics repair infrastructure.

Some in India want the right to repair.

Find out more:

Skip next section Traffic rehearsals, steep hotel prices as New Delhi gears up for BRICS

Traffic rehearsals, steep hotel prices as New Delhi gears up for BRICS

In a week from now, leaders and representatives of BRICS nations will descend upon New Delhi to attend the 18th summit of the international group which India is hosting as part of its 2026 presidency.

The summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital.

Preparations are entering their final stage ahead of the meet and Delhi is set to be a fortress with a heavy security blanket.

On Saturday, a motorcade rehearsal had been scheduled with the traffic authorities in Delhi issuing an advisory for diversions and regulated movement on key routes.

The Indian Express has reported that drones would be deployed to track the movement of traffic and spot chokepoints during the summit.

Meanwhile, media reports earlier this week said that hotel prices in the capital were soaring around the dates of the summit.

Indian news outlets said that luxury hotels in the city were either fully sold out or were giving rooms at a significantly higher tariff.

For one luxury hotel in central Delhi, a room that costs 23,000 Indian Rupees (€210, $243 approx) a night this weekend was listed at 280,000 Indian Rupees (€2,550, $2,963 approx) per night from September 10 to 13, with the rates going back to normal from September 14th, a search on a travel app showed.

India's fourth round of BRICS chairship

BRICS is an 11-member bloc which brings together major emerging markets and developing countries of the world. 

India said the upcoming meet will also be joined by partner countries and outreach invitees.

The group's presidency rotates annually among the member states.

India, which is also a founding member of BRICS, has previously held the presidency thrice — in 2012, 2016 and 2021.

India's BRICS chairship is guided by the theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," according to a statement by the foreign ministry in New Delhi.

Skip next section Indian athletes prepare for Asian Games by spending night in shipping container-like units

Indian athletes prepare for Asian Games by spending night in shipping container-like units

India's athletes are gearing up for this month's Asian Games being hosted by Japan and their preparations involve living temporarily in shipping container-style units to acclimate to their official lodgings during the continental sporting event. 

The Japanese prefecture of Aichi will stage the Games from September 19 to October 4, with over 17,000 athletes and ​officials in attendance.

The number of participants is higher than the Olympics and in a cost-cutting move, they will not stay in a traditional athletes' village but in hotels, a cruise ship and temporary units mostly made of wood.

The Sports Authority of India (SAI) has constructed similar wooden container-style accommodations at its athlete headquarters in Patiala and Bengaluru to replicate the arrangement in Japan.

In the SAI's southern Indian campus in Bengaluru, two fully air-conditioned container-style units have been built, measuring 40-foot-long (12 meters) ​and 10-foot-wide.

Each unit two small twin bedrooms, two bathrooms, a ​kitchen and ⁠a living area with a TV and music ⁠system.

Up north in Punjab's Patiala, SAI gave journalists a tour of the two cabins built there.

"These containers are like a simulator," Vineet Kumar, deputy director general of the SAI, told news agency AFP in Patiala.

"It is a unique concept as never in an Asian Games or Olympics this kind of accommodation was used," he said.

Kumar told AFP that the replicas were made to ensure that Indian athletes "don't feel the shock and get claustrophobic when they are given such accommodation in Japan."

The SAI told the media that a roster has been made for the athletes to stay for a night, turn-by-turn, before they fly out for Japan.

Skip next section India marks Teachers' Day

India marks Teachers' Day

India is celebrating its national Teachers' Day on Saturday.

Every year on September 5, educational institutions across the country hold cultural events and programs honoring teachers for their contributions to the society.

Teachers' Day in India is celebrated on the birth anniversary of renowned scholar and philosopher Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who was born on September 5, 1888 and served as the second president of the nation.

The commemoration dates back to 1962, a few months after he became president.

According to a popular anecdote, some of Radhakrishnan's students wanted to celebrate his birthday but the academic-turned-statesman is believed to have told them that it would be his "proud privilege" if the day was observed as Teachers' Day instead.

On Saturday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi extended Teachers’ Day greetings.

"#TeachersDay is about appreciating the strong contribution of teachers to our society. It is also a day to pay homage to Dr. S. Radhakrishnan," he wrote on X as he shared visuals of his meeting with the recipients of the annual National Teachers' Awards that were presented on Friday.

Skip next section Nepal floods: India says tally of missing Indians at 275

Nepal floods: India says tally of missing Indians at 275

India has said that 275 of its nationals remain missing, ten days after flash floods ravaged areas along the Nepal-Tibet border.

A total of 169 Indians have been rescued so far from the flood-affected areas in Nepal, India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Friday evening. 

Jaiswal said that in the latest rescue three Indians, including a five-year-old, were pulled to safety from Trishuli Bazaar in Nepal.

"Our Embassy in Nepal is assisting in their return to India by air," he said on X.

The spokesperson told a press conference in New Delhi that 1,907 Indian nationals have safely crossed over to Nepal from China.

No Indian travelers are now stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region, Jaiswal announced, citing official Chinese sources.

Nepal's official death toll from the deluge now stands at 1,294, with 5,053 still missing.

A frantic rescue effort has gone on for days to search for survivors, especially at mud-filled hydropower tunnels, where hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped.

Indian team assists in Rasuwa tunnel rescue

On Saturday, New Delhi's envoy to Kathmandu said that an Indian tunnel rescue team, working with Nepal's defense forces at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, had stepped up operations.

"The Indian tunnel rescue team working alongside with Nepali Army dug deeper into Chilime tunnel yesterday draining out water. A temporary track is also being made to allow more heavy equipment to reach tunnel," Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava said.

He added that doctors accompanying the Indian rescuers had also held a health camp for the local community.

India has also supplied nearly 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the floods hit the country on August 26, Jaiswal said on Friday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi from DW's studio in Delhi, bringing you the weekend edition of our India blog where we break down all the biggest headlines that are making a splash in the world's most populous nation. 

A total of 275 Indians are still missing in the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods as deaths in the disaster cross the 1,200 mark.

In diplomatic news, a countdown has begun in New Delhi for next week's BRICS summit. India is set to host leaders of member nations as the economic bloc's chair.

Meanwhile in the world of sports, Indian athletes are prepping for the Asian Games in a rather unconventional manner — by sleeping in shipping container-style units.

Stay tuned for all this and more.

entries.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
entries.summary: Germany has high-security labs while Kosovo has Hyalomma ticks and experience with the deadly Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Working together, German and Kosovar scientists are fighting the disease and its vectors.
entries.content:
September 6, 2026

Germany has high-security labs while Kosovo has Hyalomma ticks and experience with the deadly Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Working together, German and Kosovar scientists are fighting the disease and its vectors.

It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.

Seeking German cooperation

Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."

"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.

Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.

"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.

Patients require intensive care, isolation

He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

"If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.

Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.

Successful tick tactics

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.

Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.

Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.

"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."

This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
entries.summary: Several German cities will receive rapidly deployable units capable of defending against drone strikes on critical infrastructure, according to Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
entries.content:
September 6, 2026

Several German cities will receive rapidly deployable units capable of defending against drone strikes on critical infrastructure, according to Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday.

On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet.

German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied.

What did Dobrindt say about the shield?

Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves."

The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units.

The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks.

Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices.

The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage.

Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war

On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by ​and ​large, the ​start of ‌a real war."

He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats.

"All ‌these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in ‌Europe once again — they are ‌being ​put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti.

He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

New tech planned to boost cyber security

Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks.

The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs.

The newspaper said the government ⁠also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition ⁠and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks.

Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025

The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year.

These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks.

Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub.

The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery
